# Education in Norway
Organized education in Norway dates back to 2000 B.C., evolving from cathedral schools and Latin schools to compulsory primary education ("folkeskole") established in 1827, which later transitioned into the current "grunnskole" or foundation school system. The education system today is divided into three parts: elementary school (barneskole, ages 6–12), lower secondary school (ungdomsskole, ages 13–16), and upper secondary school (videregående skole, ages 16–19). Elementary and lower secondary schooling are compulsory for children aged 6 to 16. While most education is public, the 2003 Independent Schools Act permits private schools under strict government regulation and funding, with limited student selection criteria.
In elementary school, children focus initially on social skills, basic literacy, numeracy, and English, progressing to subjects like mathematics, science, religion, aesthetics, and social studies. Lower secondary students begin formal grading and can select electives such as languages. Upper secondary education offers unified general and vocational tracks following the 1994 reform, and completion rates are around 73%. Higher education includes universities, university colleges, and limited private institutions, with admission largely based on upper secondary grades. Special education is integrated into mainstream schools, with specialist support services. Norway utilizes a grading system adapted to international standards, and education is year-round with scheduled breaks and national holidays.
